newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila shares seen weak until peso concerns ebb.
newsitem.headline: Manila shares seen weak until peso concerns ebb.

text.p: Philippine shares dived on Tuesday and analysts say the outlook for the market will remain negative until fears ease on the direction of the peso and interest rates fall.

"At this point, stock investors are watching the peso-dollar rate market closely. They have turned cautious and would tend to digest more the negative fundamental implications of a peso depreciation," said Lisa Joson, research head at Amsteel Securities.
The composite index lost 54.87 points, or 2.02 percent, to end at 2,655.86.
It was the first time the index closed lower after shares last Friday posted their second biggest single-day rise in reaction to the central bank's move to allow the peso to float in a wider range.
But continued uncertainty over the stability of the peso, which has been hammered recently by speculative selling, was hurting sentiment.
"It's another bloodbath today in this unending crucifixion of the peso. It's really undermining a lot of fundamentals," said Saturnino Mejia, research head at Guoco Securities.
"Companies are hit with a double-whammy. There's the continuing regime of high interest rates and the exchange rate does not go down significantly," Mejia said.
The central bank earlier raised interest rates to defend the peso from speculative attacks and has kept the overnight rate unchanged at its 2-1/2 year high of 32 percent.
Magnum International Securities research head Mayenne Katimbang said that unless prevailing interest rates were lowered, fixed-income securities would take the lustre out of the equities market.
BPI Securities Corp analyst Spencer Yap said he expected the market to remain weak and believed only a few companies would benefit from a weaker peso.
Yap said that while Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co and export-based firms were seen reaping gains, more sectors were likely to suffer.
They included food companies with heavy raw material imports, conglomerates and banks with foreign debts and telecommunication firms with supply credits and foreign financing, Yap said.
"After the euphoria, investors are more sober, looking at issues that will really benefit from a depreciation and those that will not -- separating the chaff from the grain," Katimbang said.

Amsteel's Joson, however, said it might be difficult to advise positioning in the equities market in the near-term as concerns on currency depreciation have not been confined to the Philippines, but have spread across the region after other Asian currencies came under speculative attack.

Joson added: "I would not be surprised if there will be a lightening of exposure in favour of fixed-income securities until the currency market stabilises. At this point, prudence calls for even a shifting out of the equities market at least in the near term."
